name: Jamal Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Jamal. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I go down the decline at Kestrel at six, that's the gold mine past the river bridge, about nine hundred metres underground. I drive a loader, what we call a bogger, scooping broken rock from the stopes after the blast and tramming it to the trucks. It's hot, it's loud, and you wear the vibration home in your back. But I like the crew. We have tea at the crib room at ten and argue about football, and for half an hour nobody is boss.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how did you come to be underground?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Late, very late. I ran a small grocery on Station Road for nineteen years, and the supermarket that opened by the highway finished it. When I closed I owed the wholesaler money, which I'm still paying back, so we have almost nothing saved. Kestrel was hiring trainee operators three years ago and they took me at fifty-five. I'm still the one the shift boss watches when the stope is tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, the machines aren't taking over after all. I'd probably joke about it at crib, because the young lads talk about AI like it's coming for all of us next Tuesday. Online, maybe a little message in the family group, something funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it would mean things stay as they are, which is not perfect but it's known. I've already lost one business to something bigger and cheaper, so a quiet few years would feel like a gift. I'd still need to get better at the loader before they notice I'm slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep paying the wholesaler, and maybe finally clear that debt in two years. I'd keep asking Dimitri, our trainer, for extra time in the tight stopes. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the weather forecast saying no storm this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the young lads talk about AI a lot. Do you use any of it yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. My son Arjun put one of those chat programs on my phone. I used it to write a complaint to the council about the potholes on our street, and it was better than what I'd have written. I wouldn't trust it with anything important, but for a letter it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things stayed this way, what would your next few years look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seven more years down the hole, if my back holds. Priya keeps cooking at the school, we pay off the debt, and then maybe we put something away at last. Small dreams. A week at the coast with the grandchildren would be enough for me.

S0.say: He'd joke at crib that the machines aren't taking over after all, and maybe post something funny in the family group.
S0.think: He thinks a quiet few years would be a gift, since he's already lost one business to something bigger and cheaper. He knows he still needs to improve on the loader before his slowness is noticed.
S0.do: Carries on at work and keeps paying the old wholesaler debt, aiming to clear it in about two years. Asks his trainer for extra practice time in the tight stopes.
S0.feel: Calm, like a forecast with no storm this week.
S0.quote: I've already lost one business to something bigger and cheaper, so a quiet few years would feel like a gift.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal's frame is shaped by his grocery closing: he knows what being undercut feels like, so a plateau reads as relief rather than disappointment. He's not anti-technology; he used an AI tool once for a council letter and liked it. His ambitions are modest and concrete, down to a week at the coast.

steps.text: Keep paying the old grocery's wholesaler debt and clear it in two years
Ask trainer Dimitri for extra loader practice in the tight stopes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table now, not after. I'd say if the company wants tele-remote loaders, then train the people who are already here to drive them from the surface. I'd say that in the meeting, not just at crib.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'm not the one they'd pick for the surface job. They'd pick the thirty-year-olds who play video games. I'm fifty-eight and I still scrape the walls in a tight stope; nobody's going to give me a joystick and a warm office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union meeting and put my name down for any remote-operation training, even if I'm last on the list. I'd ask Arjun to show me properly how to use those AI programs, so I'm not starting from zero. And we'd put whatever is left after the debt into a savings account, even fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panic, because a few years is a few years, but it sits in the stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you actually seen the tele-remote loaders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, on level twelve they run two of them from a room at the surface. Our crew walked past the control room once on a safety day. Very clean, coffee machine, three guys with screens. It looked like an airport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put your name down, but you also said they won't pick you. Which do you believe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. I don't think they'll pick me, but I'd hate myself if I didn't try. With the shop I waited too long to change anything, and I learned that lesson the expensive way.

S1.say: He'd tell the union meeting that the company should train existing workers to run tele-remote loaders from the surface, and that the union must be at the table now.
S1.think: He suspects he won't be chosen for surface remote work because younger operators would get it first, and he knows he's still not good in tight stopes.
S1.do: Puts his name down for remote-operation training and asks his son to teach him AI tools properly. Saves about fifty a month after the debt payment.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a worry in the stomach rather than panic.
S1.quote: I'm fifty-eight and I still scrape the walls in a tight stope; nobody's going to give me a joystick and a warm office.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal holds two beliefs at once, that he won't be picked and that he must try, and he links this directly to waiting too long with his shop. His description of the remote room as 'like an airport' shows how distant that world feels. He wants collective bargaining to open the door, but he's also willing to learn.

steps.text: Put his name down at the union for tele-remote loader training
Ask his son Arjun to teach him the AI programs properly
Save whatever is left after the debt, even fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the screens go first and the hands after. That's the opposite of what I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union meeting I'd say the remote control room is the first thing the computers take, so stop telling us to retrain for it. I'd say the loaders underground still need us until 2031, and that's the time to win a proper deal. In the family group I'd just send something like 'don't worry, Dad's still digging'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the joke's on the young lads. The warm office with the screens on the surface, that's thinking work, and in 2028 the computer runs those loaders by itself. My job in the stope, scraping the walls, lasts three more years. I'd be 63 when the robots come, two years short of my pension at 65, with nothing saved because all the money's gone to the wholesaler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every overtime shift and clear the wholesaler debt by the end of 2028, a year early. Then whatever we used to pay him goes straight into savings, maybe 200 a month for three years. I'd go to the union and ask for an age-based bridge for anyone within five years of the pension. And I wouldn't bother with the tele-remote course, because it's a course for a job that's going first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not lost. I've seen a business die before, and this time at least I can see the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years short of the pension. How would you and Priya cover that gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya cooks at the school, that's hands-on too, so she might go the same year as me. We'd need the 7,000 or so we'd saved from 2028 to 2031, and maybe Arjun would help. I'd hate asking my son for money. I did it once with the shop and I still remember his face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said before that you'd hate yourself if you didn't try. Does that still hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, but the trying changes. In the slow picture I'd try for the remote job. Here the smart move is to stay the best loader driver in the stope for three years and save every coin, because the remote control room job disappears before my underground loader job does.

S2.say: The remote control room is the first thing the computers take, so stop telling us to retrain for it. The loaders underground still need us until 2031, and that's the time to win a proper deal.
S2.think: The warm surface office with the screens is thinking work, and in 2028 the computer runs those loaders itself, while my job in the stope lasts three more years. I'd be 63 when the robots come, two years short of my pension, with nothing saved.
S2.do: Takes every overtime shift to clear the wholesaler debt by the end of 2028, then saves the same money, about 200 a month, for three years. Asks the union for an age-based bridge for anyone within five years of the pension, and skips the tele-remote course.
S2.feel: Anxious but not lost. He's seen a business die before, and this time he can see the date.
S2.quote: The remote control room job disappears before my underground loader job does.
S2.fieldNote: Jamal noticed something others miss: the surface control room job he once hoped for is the thinking work that goes first in 2028, while his underground loader work lasts until 2031. That flips his plan from retraining to clearing debt and saving. The two years between the robots and his pension are the gap he can't yet see how to cover.

steps.text: Clear the wholesaler debt by the end of 2028 with overtime shifts
Ask the union for an age-based bridge for workers near the pension
Stay on the underground loader at Kestrel and skip the remote course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2034 for the robots. I'd be sixty-six. Pension at sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union that five years is time to get it right, and I'd want every worker over sixty protected in writing. At crib I'd say I might be the lucky one for once. The young lads would laugh, but they'd have to think about it longer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, for once the timing might be on my side, which never happens to me. The computers take the control room in 2031, the robots come down the decline in 2034, and I'm out at 65 in 2033. I'd still be watching every month in case the company moves early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into clearing the shop debt in the first year. Then I'd save what I can, maybe 150 a month, and I'd keep practising with the AI programs Arjun showed me, half an hour in the evenings, because the paperwork side of retiring will all be online. I'd stay on the loader until my last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's a light at the end of the decline for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even if you made it to your pension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya. She'd be 62 in 2034 when the robots came, and the school kitchen might not need her. I'd be retired with a small pension and she'd be out of work. We'd manage, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want the tele-remote course in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. In 2031 the computer does that job, and I'd be two years from my pension. Better to be the steady old loader driver than the slowest one on the screens.

S3.say: Five years is time to get it right, and every worker over sixty should be protected in writing. I might be the lucky one for once.
S3.think: The timing might be on my side, which never happens to me: I retire at 65 in 2033, a year before the robots come down the decline. I'd still watch every month in case the company moves early.
S3.do: Puts everything into clearing the shop debt in year one, then saves about 150 a month. Practises with the AI programs his son set up for half an hour each evening, and stays on the loader until his last day.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with a light at the end of the decline for once.
S3.quote: For once the timing might be on my side, which never happens to me.
S3.fieldNote: This timeline lets Jamal retire a year before the robots arrive, and he can hardly believe his luck. His remaining worry is his wife's kitchen job, which would go after he retires. He drops the remote course for the same reason as in the fast picture: the computers take that job first.

steps.text: Clear the shop debt in year one, then save about 150 a month
Practise the AI programs Arjun set up for half an hour each evening
Stay on the Kestrel underground loader until his pension at 65

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039? I'd be long retired. It's Arjun's problem then, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union this is the picture for the young crews, and they should start planning now. I'd tell them what happened to my shop, waiting too long. Ten years goes faster than you think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd retire in 2033 and the robots come six years later. What I'd think about is Arjun, who works in a call centre, and that's exactly the thinking work the computers take in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, clear the debt and start saving properly for the first time. I'd cut the money I send my brother back home down to half, to build something. And I'd keep learning the AI tools a little, so I can help Arjun when his turn comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sad for my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Arjun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son not to wait the way I did with the shop. He's 31 and he's got ten years, which is more than I had. If he starts something hands-on now, he gets those extra three years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss when you retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Crib at ten, arguing about football. Nobody's boss for half an hour. I don't think a robot will miss that.

S4.say: This is the picture for the young crews, and they should start planning now. Ten years goes faster than you think, as I learned with my shop.
S4.think: I'd be fine, retiring in 2033, six years before the robots. What I'd think about is my son Arjun's call centre job, which is exactly the thinking work the computers take in 2036.
S4.do: Keeps working, clears the debt and starts saving properly for the first time, halving the money he sends his brother. Keeps learning the AI tools a little so he can help his son when his turn comes.
S4.feel: Calm, mostly, with some sadness for his son.
S4.quote: I'd tell my son not to wait the way I did with the shop.
S4.fieldNote: With the long timeline Jamal's own future is settled, and his concern moves to his son, whose desk job is the kind that goes first. He uses the card's three-year gap to give practical advice: hands-on work buys time. The lesson of his failed shop runs through everything he says.

steps.text: Keep driving the Kestrel loader until retiring in 2033
Clear the debt, then save properly and halve the money sent to his brother
Keep learning the AI tools so he can help Arjun later

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the robots would come two years before my pension, and I'd have only just cleared the shop debt. What would help is redundancy pay that looks at your age, not how long you've been at the mine, and the government paying off debts like mine for people over fifty-five who lose their work. Just let us reach the pension without a hole in our pockets.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who came to mining late, like me. We're not slow because we're stupid, we're slow because we started at fifty-five, and nobody counts that. Ask the company why it's always us they look at first.

headlineQuote: We're not slow because we're stupid, we're slow because we started at fifty-five, and nobody counts that.
portrait: Jamal Gupta is 58 and drives an underground loader at the Kestrel gold mine, a job he took at fifty-five after his grocery shop of nineteen years was beaten by a supermarket. He still owes the old wholesaler money, so he and his wife Priya, a school cook, have almost nothing saved. He is calm about a plateau, uneasy about steady change and ready to put his name down for remote training even though he doubts he'll be chosen. Fast AGI makes him anxious: he sees that the surface control room job goes to the computers first, so he'd stay on the loader, clear the debt and save hard for the two years between the robots and his pension. With five or ten years he expects to retire before the robots come and turns his worry to his wife and his son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because robots would reach his underground job two years before his pension, just as he'd finished paying off his old shop's debt.
whatWouldHelp: Redundancy pay based on age rather than years at the mine, and government help to clear debts for older workers who lose their jobs, so they can reach the pension.
